findings.title: detectProvider silently picks between providers that share order 200 instead of failing, and both providers' constructors run
findings.description:
`detectProvider` sorts by `order()` descending and takes `get(0)`. `Stream.sorted` is stable, so equal orders keep ServiceLoader (classpath) order. `DefaultCryptoProvider.order()` returns 200 (crypto/default/.../DefaultCryptoProvider.java:83-84), and so do `FIPS1402Provider` (crypto/fips1402/.../FIPS1402Provider.java:114-115) and `WildFlyElytronProvider` (crypto/elytron/.../WildFlyElytronProvider.java:76-77). FIPS therefore has no preference over the default provider. The diff also removes the `size() > 1` guard that used to throw `IllegalStateException`, so a classpath that holds both now starts silently with whichever provider loads first. The `collect` instantiates every discovered provider, and both constructors have global effects: the default one registers BC (DefaultCryptoProvider.java:68-69), and the FIPS one inserts BCFIPS and BCJSSE at Security positions 1–3 and rewrites security properties (FIPS1402Provider.java:94-100). The losing provider's effects stay installed.

In the distributions I checked, this is avoided. `ClassLoaderUtil.java:40-42` loads only one crypto module for client-cli, and Quarkus uses `IgnoredArtifacts.java:51-65` plus an explicit `CryptoIntegration.setProvider` at `KeycloakRecorder.java:214`. The defect is reachable on any other classpath that contains two of these modules. Giving FIPS a strictly higher order, or keeping a fail-fast on equal top orders, would address it.

findings.title: AuthzClient.create() pins the process-wide crypto provider to the authz-client stub, which blocks later initialization
findings.description: `create(Configuration)` calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`. `init` detects only while `cryptoProvider == null` and never re-detects (common/.../CryptoIntegration.java:29-38), so the first caller's classloader decides for the whole JVM. If the authz-client loader cannot see a stronger provider, `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (order 100) is pinned. A later `init` from the application's loader, such as the one in `services/.../KeycloakApplication.java:89`, becomes a no-op, so a default or FIPS provider on that loader is never chosen. Most stub methods throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (for example `getPemUtils` at AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:84-88), so later callers fail instead of falling back. The hazard does not trigger when the crypto module shares the authz client's loader, because 200 beats 100. Quarkus's `setProvider` at `KeycloakRecorder.java:214` overwrites unconditionally, so that path is unaffected. Consider not initializing global state from client construction, or having `init` re-detect when only the fallback was found.

findings.title: Adding an abstract `order()` to the public CryptoProvider SPI breaks out-of-tree implementations once two or more providers are discovered
findings.description: `int order();` has no default body. Every in-tree implementation was updated, so the repo itself builds. Any external implementation compiled against the old interface does not define the method. When two or more providers are discovered, `detectProvider` calls `order()` on each during the sort (CryptoIntegration.java:57), so the external provider raises `AbstractMethodError` and `CryptoIntegration.init` fails for the whole process. A single-provider classpath is not affected, because the comparator is never invoked. A default implementation (for example, returning 0) would keep existing implementations loading.
